read-20260920-c60-formulations.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th edition, chapter 60, TABLE 60-8
read-20260920-c60-formulations.auditText:
2. WHERE THE INTRAVENOUS RISPERIDONE CAME FROM.

Same paragraph, page 1935, opens: if proceeding with antipsychotic administration, the intravenous route should be reserved for monitored settings due to the risk of torsades and sudden death; parenteral administration is required where rapid onset with short duration is needed, whereas oral or intramuscular use is associated with a more optimal duration of action.

So the IV sentence and the risperidone dose sit in one paragraph, three sentences apart, and the index fused them. That route sentence is about parenteral antipsychotic administration generally and haloperidol specifically. It is not about risperidone.

Table 60-8, title page 2013, rows page 2014, settles the formulations as printed. Risperidone: oral tablet, oral solution, oral disintegrating tablets — nothing parenteral. Olanzapine: tablet, disintegrating tablets, IM. Quetiapine: tablet. Aripiprazole: oral tablet, oral solution, oral disintegrating tablets. Haloperidol: oral tablet, oral solution, IM, IV. Clozapine: oral tablet. Pimavanserin: oral tablet, 34 mg. The table's own footnote defines IM as intramuscular injection and IV as intravenous, and IV appears on the haloperidol row alone. A further printed footnote: only short-acting formulations are listed; long-acting injectables exist for some antipsychotics but are not recommended for use in dementia.

TABLE 58-1, Predisposing and precipitating factors for delirium from validated predictive models. Title 1917, rows 1918.
Predisposing: dementia or cognitive impairment; comorbidity/severity of illness; depression; vision and/or hearing impairment; functional impairment; history of transient ischemia or stroke; history of alcohol abuse; history of hypertension; carotid artery disease; history of delirium; age over 70.
Precipitating: drugs (polypharmacy, psychoactive medications, sedatives, hypnotics); use of physical restraints; indwelling bladder catheter; physiologic — elevated BUN/creatinine ratio, elevated serum urea, abnormal serum albumin, abnormal sodium, glucose or potassium, metabolic acidosis; infection; iatrogenic complications; major surgical procedure (eg, aortic aneurysm repair, noncardiac thoracic surgery, neurosurgery); trauma admission; urgent admission; coma; ICU stay over 10 days.

TABLE 60-1, Neuropsychiatric symptoms. Title 1993, rows 1994.
Depression/dysphoria: low mood; tearfulness; changes in sleep, appetite, energy; negative thoughts about himself/herself.
Anxiety: frequently asking for reassurance; easily upset when separated from caregiver; worry about planned events; periods of feeling shaky, unable to relax, excessively tense; avoidance of places or situations that cause nervousness.
Apathy/indifference: indifference; disinterest in activities; poor motivation; less spontaneous, less likely to initiate conversation.
Irritability/lability: easily upset or frustrated; rapid changes in mood; impatience, difficulty coping with small delays.
Agitation/aggression: arguing; pacing; disruptive vocalizations; physical aggression; rejection of care such as bathing or changing clothes; repetitive questions.
Disinhibition: socially inappropriate comments; talking openly about very personal matters; overfamiliarity with strangers; impulsive behaviors; overeating; overspending.
Nighttime behaviors: difficulty falling asleep; early awakening; excessive nighttime awakening beyond getting up once or twice to use the bathroom and falling back asleep immediately; excessive daytime napping.
Appetite/eating: weight changes; loss or increase of appetite; change in types of food liked, eg eating too many sweets.
Motor disturbance: wandering; rummaging; pacing; doing things repeatedly such as picking at things; excessive fidgeting.
Hallucinations: can occur in any sensory modality, but visual and auditory are most common.
Delusions: false beliefs, eg that others are stealing from them or planning to harm them, that their spouse is having an affair, that family members plan on abandoning them.
Elation/euphoria: appearing excessively happy; laughing inappropriately; childish sense of humor; inflated sense of self.

TABLE 60-4, the DICE approach. Title 2004, rows 2005.
Describe, visible portion: context of behavior; social and physical environment; patient perspective; degree of distress to patient and caregiver.
Investigate, provider investigates possible causes of problem behavior: undiagnosed medical conditions; underlying psychiatric comorbidity; limitations in functional ability; one line is OCR-damaged and reads in part "poor sleep ... hygiene", which I have not reconstructed and you must not either; boredom, fear, sense of loss of control; medication side effects; sensory impairment; environmental factors; unmet needs.
Create, provider, caregiver and team collaborate to create and implement treatment plan: respond to medical problems; strategize behavioral interventions; provide caregiver education and support; create meaningful activities for the patient; simplifying tasks; ensuring the environment is safe; enhancing communication with the patient; increasing or decreasing stimulation in the environment.
Evaluate: provider evaluates whether the interventions have been implemented by the caregiver and whether they are effective.

boundary-20260920-pdcompare.shortSource: Hazzard 8e, ch. 61, TABLE 61-4 (title PDF p. 2037; rows below)
boundary-20260920-pdcompare.auditText:
1. THE DLB ONE-YEAR RULE IS NOT A TWO-WAY CONFLICT. IT IS TWO AGAINST ONE, AND THERE IS A TABLE.

TABLE 61-4, COMPARISON OF DIAGNOSTIC FEATURES FOR PD AND OTHER ATYPICAL PARKINSONIAN CONDITIONS, title p2037, rows p2038. Its DLB row lists as an inclusion feature: "Dementia within 1 y of the onset of motor features of parkinsonism".

That is the same rule as chapter 61's prose on p2035 and the opposite direction from chapter 63's p2135 wording. So the count is chapter 61 prose plus Table 61-4 on one side, chapter 63 prose on the other. Present the operative rule as dementia arising within one year of the onset of parkinsonism, cite p2035 and TABLE 61-4 at p2037/2038, and keep chapter 63's sentence visible as the outlier phrasing with its own page rather than silently dropping it. Do not cite TABLE 63-3 for any of it — I read it, it carries no temporal criterion at all.

Printed footnote to TABLE 61-4, which must travel with it: the table summarises published diagnostic criteria; the inclusion and exclusion lists are not exhaustive; for any given disease not all inclusion criteria are required to make an affirmative diagnosis; and the presence of a single exclusion criterion does not represent an absolute contraindication to diagnosing that disorder. The plus signs denote strength of association between a feature and a disorder.

TABLE 61-4 rows as printed, inclusion / supportive / exclusion:
PD — bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor, asymmetric onset (++) / gradually progressive course, good response to dopaminergic therapies (++), motor fluctuations (+++), dyskinesias (+++), motor symptom duration over 5 y / focal brain lesions within the basal ganglia, recent history of neuroleptic medication use, severe dysautonomia unrelated to medications.

2. TABLE 61-3, CRITERIA TO EXCLUDE THE DIAGNOSIS OF PARKINSON DISEASE IN FAVOR OF ANOTHER CAUSE OF PARKINSONISM, title and rows p2037. Each criterion is printed with the alternative diagnosis it points to, and that pairing is the whole value of the table — do not publish the criteria as a bare list.
History of: encephalitis — postencephalitic; exposure to carbon monoxide, manganese or other toxins — toxin induced; recent exposure to neuroleptic medications or metoclopramide — drug induced; head trauma — posttraumatic; stroke — vascular.
Presence on examination of: cerebellar ataxia — MSA, primary ataxic disorders; loss of downward ocular movements — PSP; pronounced postural hypotension not because of concurrent medication — MSA; pronounced unilateral rigidity with or without dystonia, apraxia, cortical sensory loss, alien limb — CBS; myoclonus — CBS, MSA; falling or freezing of gait early in the course of the disease — PSP; autonomic dysfunction not because of medications — MSA; excessive drooling of saliva — MSA; early dementia or hallucinations from medications — DLB; dystonia induced with low-dose levodopa — MSA; lacunar infarcts — vascular parkinsonism; capacious cerebral ventricles — normal pressure hydrocephalus; cerebellar atrophy — MSA, primary ataxic disorders; atrophy of the midbrain or other parts of the brainstem — PSP, MSA.
Effect of medication: poor response to levodopa — PSP, MSA, CBS, vascular, NPH; no dyskinesias despite high-dose levodopa — same.

boundary-20260920-referral.auditText:
3. TABLE 47-7, EXAMPLES OF CRITERIA FOR REFERRAL, title and rows p1563. Three columns: finding, definition, reason. The definitions carry the numbers and the numbers are the exam.
History — recent history of lower urinary tract or pelvic surgery or irradiation: surgery or irradiation involving the pelvic area or lower urinary tract within the past 6-12 months; seek a structural abnormality relating to the recent procedure. Recurrent symptomatic urinary tract infections: two or more symptomatic episodes in a 12-month period; exclude a structural abnormality or pathologic condition predisposing to infection.
Physical examination — marked pelvic prolapse, defined by the descent of the vaginal vault with coughing during speculum examination (the middle of this cell is OCR-damaged and I am not reconstructing the wording); marked prostatic enlargement and/or suspicion of cancer: gross enlargement on digital examination, prominent induration or asymmetry; an evaluation to exclude prostate cancer may be appropriate.
Postvoid residual — difficulty passing a 14-French straight catheter: impossible passage, or passage requiring considerable force or a large rigid catheter; anatomic blockage of the urethra or bladder neck may be present. Postvoid residual volume greater than or equal to 200 mL: volume remaining within a few minutes after the patient voids spontaneously in as normal a fashion as possible; anatomic or neurogenic obstruction or poor bladder contractility may be present.
Hematuria — greater than or equal to 3 red blood cells per high-power field (the reason cell truncates at "a pathologic condition in the upper uri-").
Therapeutic trial — failure to respond to adequate trials of behavioural and/or pharmacologic therapy: persistent symptoms bothersome to the patient after adequate trials; urodynamic evaluation may help guide specific therapy.
NOTE THE TRAP, since this project has already been bitten by it: the 200 mL here is a POSTVOID RESIDUAL referral threshold. It is not the cough-test volume. Two facts sharing a number are two facts.

boundary-20260920-uitreat.auditText:
4. TABLE 47-8, TREATMENT OPTIONS FOR URINARY INCONTINENCE IN OLDER ADULTS, title p1564, rows p1564-1565. Structure matters as much as content.
Behavioral interventions (see Table 47-10) — patient-dependent: pelvic muscle exercises, bladder training, bladder retraining; adjunctive techniques: biofeedback, electrical stimulation, weight loss; caregiver-dependent: scheduled toileting, habit training, prompted voiding.
Drugs (see Table 47-12) — bladder relaxants, alpha agonists, alpha antagonists, topical estrogen.
Surgery or procedure based — bladder neck suspension (retropubic suspension or sling procedure), removal of obstruction or pathologic lesion, sacral neuromodulation, percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation, periurethral injections, botulinum toxin A cystoscopic injections.
Mechanical devices — urethral plugs (female only), artificial sphincters, external penile clamps.
Nonspecific supportive measures — education, modifications of medication intake, avoid caffeine and alcohol, use of toilet substitutes, environmental manipulations, garments and pads, catheters (external, intermittent, indwelling).
The patient-dependent versus caregiver-dependent split is the clinically load-bearing distinction in this table and is the thing most likely to be flattened into one list. Do not flatten it.

5. TABLE 55-2 AND TABLE 55-3 ARE DIFFERENT CLINICAL ACTS and the pair is on the boundary risk list. 55-2, title and rows p1791, is a DELAY list: acute problems that postpone rehabilitation until resolved. 55-3, title p1792 rows p1793, is a GOALS list: durable factors that change what rehabilitation can achieve.
TABLE 55-2, factor and reason for possible delay: delirium or altered level of consciousness — unable to cooperate or learn; hemodynamic instability — may make it unsafe to carry out certain types of exercise; occult fracture and bony metastasis — weightbearing or resistance exercise could worsen or cause fracture; acute infections such as bladder infection and pneumonia — may cause confusion, fatigue and/or hypotension; acute skin or joint infection — may cause fatigue, pain and/or muscle splinting; acute inflammatory disease such as certain rheumatologic and neuromuscular conditions — resistive exercises may impair recovery; acute orthopedic conditions — joint instability may preclude certain exercises and functional goals may be limited.
TABLE 55-3, factor and influence: cognitive impairment — goals may be more limited, take advantage of skills the patient already has, use interventions that do not require carryover; disability present for many years — goals more limited and directed to compensatory strategies or treatment of deconditioning; motivation is limited — goals need to be well defined and reached in measurable steps; patient had prior rehabilitation for the same problem — rehabilitation may be limited unless new functional decline has occurred; terminal illness — intervention directed toward reducing caregiver burden and patient discomfort; severity of disability — extremely mild disability may not require intervention, extremely severe disability may have very limited potential for benefit; social and cultural circumstances — absence of a caregiver, financial limitations and cultural beliefs may preclude certain techniques or technologies; malnutrition — unable to build muscle, rehabilitative interventions may be limited unless nutritional status is improved.
Supporting prose p1791-1792: other determinants of rehabilitation benefit include motivation, cognition and prior functional status; the worked example is a patient with COPD on home oxygen who falls and fractures a hip and may not tolerate more than 5 minutes of therapy at one time, so the approach changes to frequent short walks by therapy and nursing rather than hour-long sessions twice a day.

boundary-20260920-hypnotics.auditText:
6. TABLE 44-5, PRESCRIPTION MEDICATIONS COMMONLY USED FOR INSOMNIA IN OLDER ADULTS, title p1462, rows p1462. Columns: medication, starting dose mg, dose range mg, half-life h, comments. Classes as printed, in order.
Intermediate-acting benzodiazepine — temazepam 7.5 starting, 7.5-30 range, half-life 8.8; psychomotor impairment, increased risk of falls.
Short-acting nonbenzodiazepines — eszopiclone 1, range 1-2, half-life 6; reportedly effective for long-term use in selected individuals, may be associated with unpleasant taste and headache, avoid administration with a high-fat meal. Zaleplon 5, range 5-10, half-life 1 and reported unchanged in older adults; reportedly little daytime carryover, tolerance or rebound. Zolpidem 5, range 5, comments report little daytime carryover, tolerance or rebound insomnia — ITS HALF-LIFE CELL IS OCR-DAMAGED and stays PENDING; the decimal-dropping behaviour on this page is the same one that made me refuse darifenacin and fesoterodine, and a hypnotic half-life is not a number to guess.
Melatonin receptor agonist — ramelteon 8, range 8, half-life 1.5 and 2.6 in older adults; dizziness, myalgia, headache and other adverse events reported, no significant rebound insomnia or withdrawal on discontinuation.
Sedating antidepressants — doxepin 3, range 3-6 (the range cell is partly damaged, treat the upper bound as pending), half-life 15.3 for doxepin and 31 for the metabolite; somnolence/sedation, nausea and upper respiratory tract infection reported, antagonises central H1 receptors, active metabolite, should not be taken within 2 h of a meal. Mirtazapine 7.5, range 7.5-45, half-life 31-39 in older adults and 13-34 in younger adults; increased appetite, weight gain, headache, dizziness, daytime carryover, used for insomnia with depression. Trazodone 25-50 starting, range 25-150, half-life reportedly 6 plus or minus 2 and prolonged in older adults and obese individuals; moderate orthostatic effects, administration after food minimises sedation and postural hypotension, used for insomnia with depression.
Dual orexin receptor antagonists — lemborexant 5, range 5-10, half-life 17-19. Suvorexant starting dose cell damaged (PENDING), range 10-20, half-life 12. Both: next-day drowsiness, complex sleep-related disorder, abnormal dreams and sleep paralysis may occur; metabolism through CYP3A4.
Prescribing rule printed immediately above the table, p1462: when a sedative-hypnotic is used in older individuals, choose the smallest dose of the agent with the least risk of adverse events for the shortest duration necessary; short-acting drugs for trouble falling asleep, intermediate-acting for trouble staying asleep.
Class prose p1463, all text-layer verified: temazepam, lorazepam, triazolam and estazolam are the intermediate-acting agents most commonly used, triazolam is the shorter-acting one also used; flurazepam and quazepam should not be used in older adults because of next-day effects; benzodiazepines decrease time to fall asleep by about 10 minutes on average and reduce awakenings, increasing total sleep time by 30 to 60 minutes; side effects include confusion, falls, rebound insomnia, tolerance and withdrawal; benzodiazepines have been linked to increased pneumonia in Alzheimer disease; all are on the Beers list. NBRAs bind selectively to GABA-A, produce sedation and amnesia without anxiolysis, similar efficacy to benzodiazepines with a somewhat better side-effect profile; zolpidem and zaleplon should only be taken immediately before bed because of rapid onset; eszopiclone has the longest duration of the three and is better for sleep maintenance but may cause morning drowsiness; extended-release zolpidem exists for maintenance insomnia; complex sleep-related behaviours such as sleep driving and sleep eating have been seen with zolpidem and may be a class effect; NBRAs are also on the Beers list. Ramelteon is selective for MT1/MT2 rather than GABA, reduces total sleep latency and increases sleep time in older adults with fewer side effects.

recovery-20260920-falltable.auditText: Individually prescribed home exercise: three times per week; standing and walking with one foot directly in front of the other; toe and heel walking; walking backward, sideways and turning; stepping over an object; bending and picking up an object; stairs in the home; sit-to-stand; knee squats; moderate-intensity strengthening with ankle cuff weights; walking programme. LiFE: integrate balance and strength into daily activities whenever opportunities arise, rather than a scheduled exercise set; reduce base of support, move to limits of sway, shift weight foot-to-foot, step over objects, turn and change direction. Hybrid home-group: progressive group classes plus home programme; individually tailored dynamic balance, strength, bone, endurance, flexibility, gait and functional skills; home strength and balance twice weekly. Tai chi: group controlled leaning, multidirectional weight shift, body alignment awareness, coordinated arms/legs/trunk movement.

recovery-20260920-fallsprose.auditText: Rapid stepping training aimed at improving a key balance recovery response reduced falls by 52% in a meta-analysis of seven RCTs. On the same page a home-based programme in older people recently discharged from hospital increased falls by 43%. Greater effects occur with high challenge to balance and three or more hours/week of prescribed exercise. Exercise reduces falls even in subgroups aged 75 years and older, in group or individual settings, led by a health professional or trained exercise leader.

recovery-20260920-continence.auditText: Effective lower urinary tract function: Storage—bladder accommodates increasing volume at low pressure; closed outlet; appropriate fullness sensation; no involuntary contractions. Emptying—bladder capable of contraction; no anatomical flow obstruction; coordinated lowering of outlet resistance with contractions. Four separate non-urinary requirements at the same level as lower urinary tract function: adequate mobility/dexterity to use toilet; cognition to recognise toileting needs; motivation to be continent; no environmental or iatrogenic barriers. Title p1547, rows p1548.

recovery-20260920-physiology.source: Hazzard 8e, chapter 47, Bladder filling and emptying physiology
recovery-20260920-physiology.shortSource: Hazzard 8e, ch. 47, Bladder filling and emptying physiology
recovery-20260920-physiology.auditText: Text-layer verified: sacral spinal cord reflex governs urination. During filling, afferent pathways convey bladder volume and motor output adjusts; sympathetic tone closes the bladder neck and inhibits parasympathetic tone, relaxing the bladder dome, while somatic innervation maintains pelvic floor/striated periurethral tone. Voluntary pelvic floor contraction inhibits parasympathetic tone. Emptying: sympathetic/somatic tone diminish and parasympathetic cholinergic impulses contract the bladder. Filling pressure stays below 15 cm H2O. The first-urge volume sentence truncates at generally occurs at between 150; the range must stay pending and must not be completed.

ch60expand-20260920-table2.auditText:
TABLE 60-2, COMMON CONTRIBUTING CAUSES OF NEUROPSYCHIATRIC SYMPTOMS. Title p1997, rows p1998.
A biological stress or delirium due to a recurrent or new medical condition. A psychiatric syndrome that is either recurrent or associated with the dementia. Reaction to cognitive disturbance (eg, reaction due to inability to express oneself). An environmental stressor (eg, excessive stimulation, unfamiliar surroundings). Unmet needs (eg, hunger, thirst, pain, constipation). Sensory deficit (eg, unable to see or hear properly without the use of eyeglasses or hearing aids). Unsophisticated caregiving (eg, poor communication, rushing patient). Medication side effects.

ch60expand-20260920-table3.auditText:
TABLE 60-3, MEDICATIONS WITH ANTICHOLINERGIC ACTIVITY, WHICH HAVE INCREASED RISK OF CAUSING DELIRIUM. Title p1999, rows p2000. Printed with brand names, which are worth keeping because several of these are not recognised as anticholinergic by most readers:
Amantadine (Symadine), benztropine (Cogentin), cyproheptadine (Periactin), digoxin (Lanoxin), diphenhydramine (Benadryl), dipyridamole (Persantine), doxylamine (Aldex, Doxytex, Nitetime Sleep-Aid, Sleep Aid, Unisom), furosemide (Lasix), hydroxyzine (Vistaril, Atarax), low-potency antipsychotics, meclizine (Dramamine), metoclopramide (Reglan), oxybutynin (Ditropan), prochlorperazine (Compazine), promethazine (Phenergan), ranitidine (Zantac), scopolamine (Transderm-V), theophylline (Aerolate), tricyclic antidepressants.
Present this one so digoxin, furosemide, theophylline, dipyridamole and ranitidine are visible rather than buried mid-list. Those five are the teaching point of the table — the ones nobody expects on an anticholinergic list — and a plain alphabetical run hides exactly what makes it worth reading.
Chapter prose p1999 that belongs with it: classes most likely associated with delirium, largely due to anticholinergic effects, are opiates, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, muscle relaxants and antiepileptic medications; behavioural changes may include sedation, changes in sleep-wake cycle, and worse confusion or agitation; dopaminergic agents used in Parkinson disease can precipitate impulsive behaviours; anticholinergics, amantadine, dopaminergic agents and COMT inhibitors can exacerbate psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions.

ch60expand-20260920-table5.auditText:
TABLE 60-5, SUPPORTIVE CARE FOR THE PATIENT WITH DEMENTIA. Title p2006, rows p2007.
Carefully evaluate the patient's dementia-related needs. Provide education about the diagnosis and trajectory of dementia to the patient (if appropriate) and caregiver. Manage medical comorbidities: encourage routine follow-up with primary care, dental, vision and hearing specialists; assist with medical decision making. Address safety needs, particularly regarding falls, wandering, driving, ability to live alone, environmental hazards (eg, access to weapons, removing items patients may stumble upon), and medication management; consider obtaining a home safety evaluation and driving evaluation; encourage the use of monitoring devices. Provide comfort and emotional support. Provide meaningful activities, stimulation and socialisation, which may be achieved through adult day care, senior centres and in-home activities. Maintain and document wishes for end-of-life care and distribution of finances after death; these should be addressed while individuals still have decision-making capacity. Provide quality nursing care in advanced stages.
Prose p2007: caregiver education and skills training in communication for dementia can significantly improve patient quality of life and increase positive interactions; a recent meta-analysis found the most beneficial interventions address caregiving competency first and then gradually address the patient's care needs; in the United States about 25% of people with dementia receive care from nonfamily caregivers such as home health aides or nursing assistants hired directly by the family; for nonfamily caregivers, facility staff training programmes have been associated with reduction of NPS in patients and with staff wellbeing.

ch60expand-20260920-table6.auditText:
TABLE 60-6, GENERAL BEHAVIORAL STRATEGIES FOR COMMON NEUROPSYCHIATRIC SYMPTOMS. Title p2008, rows p2009. Two columns, symptom then strategies. This is the most directly usable table in the chapter.
Disorientation or confusion with person/object recognition — provide reminders, cues or prompts; identify individuals if the patient does not remember names or has aphasia; use environmental cues (eg, calendars, keeping blinds raised during the day, keeping lights off at night); keep objects for individual tasks in separate, labelled containers; use simple visual reminders (eg, pictures, arrows pointing to the bathroom).
Confusion or overwhelmed with tasks and environment — eliminate noise and distractions while the patient is engaged in an activity; break each task into very simple steps; offer simple choices, no more than two at a time; provide simple verbal commands, using only one or two steps at a time; remove unnecessary items from the room while the patient is engaged in a task; provide daily, structured and predictable routines.
Wandering or inability to respond appropriately to an emergency — provide 24-hour supervision; place locks on all exits; develop an emergency plan and inform neighbours, fire department and police of the patient's condition; provide medical alert and safe return ID bracelets.
Nighttime wakefulness — encourage good sleep hygiene (avoid stimulating activity, reduce caffeinated and alcoholic beverages that may affect sleep, limit daytime napping); create a quiet routine for bedtime; evaluate the environment for modifiable elements such as temperature, noise level, light, shadows and bed comfort.
Anxiety, irritability, repetitive questioning, frustration — use a relaxed and reassuring voice and light touch to help calm or redirect; avoid negative words and tone; allow the patient sufficient time to respond to questions; help the patient with aphasia find the words to express him/herself; allow extra time for tasks and activities; distract the patient as necessary; understand that behaviours are not always intentional.
Boredom and restlessness — create a structured daily schedule that includes entertainment and exercise; provide meaningful activities that draw on preserved capabilities and interests; engage patients in activities involving repetitive motion (eg, folding towels, putting items in containers).
Delusions and hallucinations — go along with the patient's point of view of what is true, avoid arguing or trying to reason as this can make the situation worse; ignore symptoms that are not distressing the person; distract the patient as necessary.
Apathy — give the patient a job at home, such as folding laundry; focus on the process of doing things rather than the results.
Disinhibition — distract from an inappropriate topic by calmly and firmly changing the subject; avoid television shows with violence or sexual content.

ch60expand-20260920-table7.auditText:
TABLE 60-7, GENERAL GUIDELINES FOR STARTING PSYCHOTROPIC MEDICATIONS FOR NEUROPSYCHIATRIC SYMPTOMS. Title p2011, rows p2012.
Explore potential contributing factors for neuropsychiatric symptoms; consider the need for a medical work-up. Define specific targets for intervention. Implement nonpharmacologic interventions concomitantly. Be mindful that isolated neuropsychiatric disturbances are unlikely to respond to medications. Use medications sparingly, starting at a low dose, monitoring for adverse effects (particularly delirium, sedation, orthostasis, falls), and using the lowest effective dose. Change one medication at a time to allow for a clearer picture of how it affects target symptoms and to minimise adverse effects. Be aware of potential drug-drug interactions. Consider timing doses around difficult behaviours (eg, administering a dose half an hour prior to morning care). Psychotropic use, particularly antipsychotics, should be time-limited, as symptoms may resolve. Obtain informed consent prior to starting medications; routinely review the risk-benefit ratio of treatment with patients and caregivers. Have a plan in place to manage after-hours crisis.

ch60expand-20260920-table9.auditText:
TABLE 60-9, ANTIDEPRESSANT ORAL DOSAGES AND SIDE EFFECTS. Title p2015, rows p2016. Columns: medication, initial daily dose mg, maximum daily dose mg, side effects. Printed footnote: maximum recommended dosage is for patients greater than 60 years of age.
SSRIs — citalopram 5-10 initial, 20 max; escitalopram 5, 10; fluoxetine 10 initial, MAXIMUM CELL PENDING, see below; sertraline 25, 200; paroxetine 10, 40; paroxetine CR 12.5, 50.
SNRIs — duloxetine 30, 120; venlafaxine XR 75, 225; venlafaxine IR 25-50, 375; desvenlafaxine 50, 100.
Other — mirtazapine 7.5, 30-45; bupropion XL 150, 450; bupropion SR 100, 150 BID; bupropion IR 75, 150 TID.
Preferred tricyclic antidepressants — nortriptyline 10-25, 75-150; desipramine 10-25, 50-150.
Side effects as printed: citalopram, GI distress, sexual dysfunction, slight weight gain, QTc PROLONGATION AT DOSES OF 20 MG OR MORE, hyponatraemia, SIADH — note that this sits in the same row as a 20 mg maximum, so the caution and the ceiling are the same number and must not be merged into one statement. Escitalopram and sertraline, GI distress, sexual dysfunction, slight weight gain, hyponatraemia, SIADH, and for sertraline headache. Fluoxetine, the same plus abnormal dreams, insomnia, fatigue. Paroxetine and paroxetine CR, anticholinergic effects may increase risk of delirium, may cause withdrawal effects due to short half-life, GI distress, hyponatraemia, SIADH. Duloxetine, GI distress, dry mouth, urinary hesitancy, headaches, fatigue, sedation, hyponatraemia, hepatic effects. Venlafaxine XR and IR, GI distress, minimal sedation, headaches, sexual dysfunction, weight loss, withdrawal symptoms, anxiety, DOSE-DEPENDENT HYPERTENSION, hyponatraemia, mild anticholinergic effects. Desvenlafaxine, dizziness, dry mouth, decreased appetite, GI distress, dose-dependent hypertension, elevated cholesterol and triglycerides, hyponatraemia. Mirtazapine, dry mouth, GI distress, dizziness, QT prolongation, elevated cholesterol and triglycerides, weight gain, increased appetite, sedation. Bupropion, minimal anticholinergic effects, hypertension, slight sexual dysfunction, serotonin syndrome, increased appetite, dry mouth — the sedation descriptor in this cell is OCR-damaged and I am not reconstructing it. Nortriptyline, THERAPEUTIC WINDOW 50-150 ng/mL, anticholinergic effects, hypotension, sedation, sexual dysfunction, slight weight gain. Desipramine, THERAPEUTIC WINDOW 150-300 ng/mL, mild anticholinergic effects, hypotension, slight GI distress, sedation, sexual dysfunction, slight weight gain.
FLUOXETINE'S MAXIMUM DAILY DOSE STAYS PENDING. Four crops at 500, 900 and 1200 dpi returned it as "8", "Hi" and "14 Hi". Its initial dose read 10 twice and is fine. The maximum is not readable and I am not filling it in.

ch60expand-20260920-oldapproval.auditText: Chapter 60 p2009 states that while psychotropics are frequently prescribed for NPS in dementia, there are currently no pharmacotherapies with US FDA approval for this purpose. neuro-20260920-agents.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 61
neuro-20260920-agents.auditText:
TABLE 61-5, DOPAMINERGIC AGENTS, title p2044, is a CLASSIFICATION list, not a dose table — do not build it as one. As printed: dopamine precursor, levodopa. Peripheral decarboxylase inhibitors, carbidopa and benserazide. Dopamine agonists, pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine, apomorphine. COMT inhibitors, entacapone and opicapone. Dopamine releaser, amantadine. Peripheral dopamine receptor blocker, domperidone. MAO type B inhibitors, selegiline, selegiline orally disintegrating, rasagiline, safinamide. A2A antagonist, istradefylline.
Combination products p2044: Sinemet is carbidopa plus levodopa; Madopar is benserazide plus levodopa; a carbidopa/levodopa formulation dissolving under the tongue and entering the stomach via swallowed saliva is useful in swallowing difficulty. Immediate release gives a more rapid and predictable "on"; extended release gives a slightly longer plasma half-life with slower, less predictable onset; the two can be combined.

neuro-20260920-tradeoff.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 61
neuro-20260920-tradeoff.auditText: THE SINGLE MOST GERIATRIC SENTENCE IN THE CHAPTER, p2045, and it must be presented as a two-way trade-off rather than a rule: dopamine agonists are more likely than levodopa to cause hallucinations, confusion and psychosis especially in older adults, so IT IS SAFER TO USE LEVODOPA IN PATIENTS OLDER THAN 70 YEARS — while agonists are LESS likely to produce dyskinesias and the wearing-off phenomenon, attributed to their lower potency and longer half-life. Two directions, one decision. A reader who carries only half of it answers the wrong way.

neuro-20260920-drugs.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 61
neuro-20260920-drugs.auditText:
Entacapone: extends levodopa's plasma half-life and increases peak plasma concentration, prolonging each dose's duration; indication is reducing motor fluctuations, increasing "on" and reducing "off"; because it enhances levodopa efficacy it can increase dyskinesias and the levodopa dose may need lowering; very short acting, one 200-mg tablet taken simultaneously with each levodopa dose; combined with carbidopa/levodopa as Stalevo.
Tolcapone: 100- and 200-mg tablets; more potent, longer duration, but greater risk of diarrhoea and hepatotoxicity, the latter having led to its removal from the US market.
Ergot agonists pergolide, bromocriptine, cabergoline: potential to induce fibrosis — cardiac valvulopathy, and retroperitoneal, pleuropulmonary and pericardial fibrosis; not recommended; pergolide withdrawn from the US market.
Pramipexole and ropinirole: equally effective at therapeutic levels; slow-release preparations available. Problems more likely with agonists than levodopa: sudden sleep attacks including falling asleep at the wheel, daytime drowsiness, ankle oedema, and impulse control problems — hypersexuality, compulsive gambling, shopping, binge eating.
Rotigotine: newest agonist, dermal patch to upper torso or arms; useful in swallowing difficulty; may smooth motor fluctuations and nocturnal akinesia when the last pre-bedtime levodopa dose does not last the night; high-potency agonist at D1, D2, D3 with lower potency at D4 and D5, so it DIFFERS from ropinirole and pramipexole which lack D1 and D5 activity, and RESEMBLES apomorphine, which has greater efficacy in PD than other agonists; the preferential D1 agonism may explain its higher efficacy for freezing of gait; transdermal delivery gives steadier levels.
Apomorphine: may be the most powerful dopamine agonist; intense nausea; historically subcutaneous; used for faster relief of a disabling "off" state; a sublingual film (Kynmobi) is now available and may suit precipitous motor fluctuations.
Amantadine: mild antimuscarinic effects, activates dopamine release, blocks dopamine uptake, blocks NMDA receptors; relieves symptoms in approximately two-thirds of patients; can induce livedo reticularis, ankle oedema, visual hallucinations, confusion; ITS ANTIGLUTAMATERGIC ACTION MAKES IT THE ONLY ESTABLISHED EFFECTIVE ANTIDYSKINETIC AGENT; anti-PD dose usually 100 mg twice daily, antidyskinetic effect requires 300 to 400 mg/day, and the antidyskinetic effect tends to lessen over time; older individuals often tolerate it poorly because of confusion and hallucinations. Two doses for two purposes in one drug — present them together or the distinction is lost.
Domperidone: peripherally active dopamine receptor blocker, prevents GI upset from levodopa and agonists; not available in the United States, available elsewhere including Canada.
MAO-B inhibitors selegiline, rasagiline, safinamide: mildly effective symptomatic benefit, without the hypertensive diet-linked effects of MAO-A inhibitors, so usable with levodopa; numerous well-powered trials failed to convincingly demonstrate neuroprotection, though interpretation is complicated because both do have symptomatic benefit; SELEGILINE, BUT NOT RASAGILINE, IS METABOLISED TO L-AMPHETAMINE AND METHAMPHETAMINE; both reduce the severity of motor fluctuations; safinamide is thought to offer greater MAO-B specificity, which in theory reduces off-target diet-related effects.

neuro-20260920-wearing.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 61
neuro-20260920-wearing.auditText:
WEARING-OFF HAS A PRINTED DEFINITION, p2047: an adequate dose of levodopa does not last at least 6 hours and bradykinesia, rigidity or tremor emerge or worsen. In the first couple of years there is a long-duration response so dose timing is unimportant; over time the long-duration response is lost, only a short-duration response remains, and wearing-off appears; "off" episodes are mild at first and become more frequent or severe.
Peak-dose dyskinesias: occur when dopamine concentration is too high; reduce the individual dose, though more frequent smaller doses may then be needed; or add amantadine starting 100 mg BID up to 200 mg BID; buspirone up to 20 mg/day may benefit dyskinesias in some patients.
PD psychosis: reduce total dopaminergic dose as far as tolerated; review medications for other agents worsening encephalopathy including benzodiazepines, anticholinergics and opioids; adjunctive treatment quetiapine starting 25 mg at bedtime, or pimavanserin 17 mg one to two times daily with dosing reduced in patients on CYP3A4 inhibitors; pimavanserin is an inverse agonist and antagonist at 5-HT2A receptors and, unlike quetiapine, has prospective clinical trial data supporting efficacy.
REM sleep behaviour disorder: mainstay is CLONAZEPAM 0.5-2 mg at bedtime, effective and well tolerated by the majority; melatonin, though less effective, may be tried first and can be combined with clonazepam; cholinesterase inhibitors may help some; DOPAMINERGIC THERAPY PROBABLY HAS LITTLE OR NO EFFECT ON RBD — that last one is counterintuitive and is the reason the item gets asked. Safety measures: separate beds, mattresses on the floor, sleeping on the first floor, removing dangerous objects from the bedroom; reviewing antidepressants that can precipitate or exacerbate RBD may be worthwhile.

neuro-20260920-tdp.auditText: TDP-43 neuropathology has four types, A to D, by inclusion pattern in nucleus and cytoplasm. Type A, often progranulin mutations, though sporadic cases occur. Type B, often motor neuron disease, and C9orf72, the commonest mutation in familial FTD-ALS, usually shows type B. TDP-C, the pattern associated with svPPA. Type D, the rare valosin mutation.

neuro-20260920-genes.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 63
neuro-20260920-genes.auditText:
MAPT, 1998: responsible for familial FTD with Parkinson disease (FTDP-17); more common in Southern Europe and France than Northern Europe; a few mutations reported in China and Japan.
PROGRANULIN (GRN), 2006: lies only 1.7 Mb from the tau gene; accounts for UP TO 11% OF SPORADIC AND 25% OF FAMILIAL FTD; onset later than tau, range 35 to 80 years; APPROXIMATELY 10% OF CARRIERS REMAIN ASYMPTOMATIC AFTER AGE 70; phenotype more variable than MAPT — bvFTD, nfvPPA, CBD, Parkinson disease, AD; ASYMMETRY IS COMMON, sometimes one hemisphere massively atrophic and the other relatively normal; AUTOIMMUNITY IS SEEN IN MORE THAN 10% OF CARRIERS AND CAN PRECEDE NEUROLOGIC DISEASE.
C9ORF72, 2011: major cause of familial FTD, ALS and FTD-ALS; a large hexanucleotide repeat expansion in an intron leads to RNA overproduction and dipeptides generated in a non-ATG manner; onset typically in the SIXTH DECADE, with fourth- and eighth-decade cases described; THE ILLNESS CAN BEGIN AS A PSYCHIATRIC ILLNESS, ranging from borderline personality disorder, bipolar illness, depression and conversion disorder to drug addiction; whether a carrier is diagnosed with bvFTD or ALS is variable and both can emerge together.
FTLD AND ALS: ABOUT 15% OF FTLD PATIENTS DEVELOP ALS; ABOUT 50% OF ALS PATIENTS DEVELOP COGNITIVE AND BEHAVIOURAL SYMPTOMS OF FTLD, a smaller percentage of these developing dementia. SOD1 was previously thought the main cause of ALS before C9orf72 was found. Two percentages, same relationship, opposite directions — keep them adjacent and labelled or they will be remembered as one number.

neuro-20260920-ppa.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 63
neuro-20260920-ppa.auditText:
THE THREE PPA SYNDROMES. As a group, greater left than right atrophy of the perisylvian region, anterior temporal lobes and basal ganglia; inferior parietal lobule atrophy is associated with predominantly word-finding deficits.
LOGOPENIC (lvPPA), named by Gorno-Tempini and colleagues: USUALLY A LANGUAGE PRESENTATION OF ALZHEIMER DISEASE, supported by clinical, genetic and imaging studies; decreased speech output, slow speech with impaired syntactic comprehension and naming; short-term phonologic memory deficits with profound echoic memory deficits — forgetting portions of longer phrases during repetition tasks.
NONFLUENT (nfvPPA): apraxic, laboured speech with grammatical errors and difficulty with complex syntax; speech apraxia is the inability to produce speech from difficulty programming the sensorimotor commands for positioning and moving speech muscles, causing difficulty initiating speech, sound substitutions, omissions, syllable transpositions, slower rate with inappropriate starts and stops, distortions that can include sounds absent from the native language, ERRORS TYPICALLY INCONSISTENT, worse for multisyllabic words; speech apraxia localises to the LEFT OPERCULAR AND ANTERIOR INSULAR REGION; anomia variably present, phonemic paraphasias frequent, dropped articles, SENTENCES TEND TO HAVE MORE NOUNS THAN VERBS; single word comprehension and semantic knowledge MAINTAINED, so nfvPPA is NOT likely in a patient with preserved articulation, preserved grammar and deficits in semantic knowledge; insight can be exquisitely preserved and depression is common, other behavioural problems uncommon early; MRI shows asymmetrically left-dominant atrophy with preferential involvement of inferior frontal lobe, insular region and caudate, FDG-PET shows left frontal hypometabolism; MOST SHOW TAU PATHOLOGY AT AUTOPSY, CBD COMMONEST THEN PSP THEN PICK, AND APPROXIMATELY 20% SHOW TDP PATHOLOGY, USUALLY TDP-43 TYPE A; as it progresses nfvPPA patients develop features of PSP, CBD or even ALS, so attention to emerging motor symptoms helps predict the underlying pathology.
SEMANTIC (svPPA): fluent, grammatically accurate speech with the hallmark loss of semantic knowledge — encyclopedic knowledge of people, objects, facts and words which, unlike episodic memory, carries no awareness of where or when it was learned; patients eventually lose all knowledge of the fact or word and show MULTIMODALITY AGNOSIA, so even given the name the object is not recognised; early on patients are often aware of word-finding and comprehension difficulty; semantic paraphasias frequent with supraordinate substitutions and nonspecific grouping words such as "stuff" and "things"; REPETITION AND PROSODY PRESERVED, as are syntax and verb recognition; SURFACE DYSLEXIA — difficulty pronouncing irregularly spelled words such as "gnat", "heir" or "pint"; difficulty with category fluency and confrontational naming, particularly low-frequency words; a RIGHT HEMISPHERIC VARIANT has been described with difficulty naming and recognising famous people and behavioural symptoms resembling bvFTD; IN CONTRAST TO AD, MANY svPPA PATIENTS HAVE GREATER DEFICITS FOR REMOTE THAN RECENT MEMORY; of all PPA syndromes svPPA has the greatest propensity for behavioural problems, supportive in diagnostic criteria — hyperorality, disinhibition, aberrant motor behaviour, loss of sympathy and empathy, narrowed preoccupations, and parsimony, with striking rigidity in thinking.

primary-neuro-pimavanserin.auditText: The US label recommends pimavanserin 34 mg orally once daily without titration for hallucinations and delusions associated with Parkinson disease psychosis. Reduce to 10 mg once daily with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors; avoid strong or moderate CYP3A4 inducers. It warns about QT prolongation and increased mortality in older patients with dementia-related psychosis. The approval excludes dementia psychosis unrelated to Parkinson disease. Read highlights, sections 2.1, 2.3 and 5.

primary-neuro-amantadine.auditText: Amantadine is renally eliminated and accumulates when kidney function declines. The label calls for dose reduction in renal impairment and in people aged 65 years or older, with possible additional reduction for heart failure, edema or orthostatic hypotension. Read Renal Disease and Usage in the Elderly. These precautions qualify the book’s regimens; they do not establish the book’s doses as default geriatric prescriptions.

primary-neuro-tolcapone.auditText: The US label lists tolcapone as an NDA authorized generic and describes 100 mg tablets. Its boxed warning reserves use ordinarily for levodopa/carbidopa patients with fluctuations who have not responded satisfactorily to, or are unsuitable for, other adjuncts because potentially fatal liver failure can occur. Liver evaluation and monitoring are required. This is evidence against teaching the supplied US-withdrawal assertion as current fact, not confirmation of pharmacy stock.

neuro-20260920-pimavanserin-historical.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 61
neuro-20260920-pimavanserin-historical.auditText:
WEARING-OFF HAS A PRINTED DEFINITION, p2047: an adequate dose of levodopa does not last at least 6 hours and bradykinesia, rigidity or tremor emerge or worsen. In the first couple of years there is a long-duration response so dose timing is unimportant; over time the long-duration response is lost, only a short-duration response remains, and wearing-off appears; "off" episodes are mild at first and become more frequent or severe.
Peak-dose dyskinesias: occur when dopamine concentration is too high; reduce the individual dose, though more frequent smaller doses may then be needed; or add amantadine starting 100 mg BID up to 200 mg BID; buspirone up to 20 mg/day may benefit dyskinesias in some patients.
PD psychosis: reduce total dopaminergic dose as far as tolerated; review medications for other agents worsening encephalopathy including benzodiazepines, anticholinergics and opioids; adjunctive treatment quetiapine starting 25 mg at bedtime, or pimavanserin 17 mg one to two times daily with dosing reduced in patients on CYP3A4 inhibitors; pimavanserin is an inverse agonist and antagonist at 5-HT2A receptors and, unlike quetiapine, has prospective clinical trial data supporting efficacy.
REM sleep behaviour disorder: mainstay is CLONAZEPAM 0.5-2 mg at bedtime, effective and well tolerated by the majority; melatonin, though less effective, may be tried first and can be combined with clonazepam; cholinesterase inhibitors may help some; DOPAMINERGIC THERAPY PROBABLY HAS LITTLE OR NO EFFECT ON RBD — that last one is counterintuitive and is the reason the item gets asked. Safety measures: separate beds, mattresses on the floor, sleeping on the first floor, removing dangerous objects from the bedroom; reviewing antidepressants that can precipitate or exacerbate RBD may be worthwhile.

coverage-20260920-pressure-mechanism.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 46
coverage-20260920-pressure-mechanism.auditText: PRESSURE, p1504-1506 region: pressure is the perpendicular force or load exerted on a specific area; the gravitational pull on the skeleton causes loading and deformation of the soft tissue between the bony prominence and the external support surface. PIs are the result of mechanical injury to the cell membrane of the muscle, directly deformed or destroyed by high-magnitude pressure such as a person lying on the floor after a fractured hip. As the soft tissue available for compression decreases the pressure gradient increases, which is why most PIs occur over bony prominences. DEFORMATION OF TISSUES IS A KEY FACTOR IN DEEP TISSUE PRESSURE INJURY AND FULL-THICKNESS PI (STAGES 3 AND 4) AND MAY BE THE FORCE THAT INITIATES CELL DEATH. Degree of deformation depends on the tissues (size and shape of layers), their mechanical properties (stiffness, strength, shape of the bone), and the magnitude and distribution of external force. The ability to withstand deformation changes with age, lifestyle, injury or disease.

coverage-20260920-strain-preparations.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 46
coverage-20260920-strain-preparations.auditText:
TWO STRAIN NUMBERS THAT MUST NOT BE MERGED, and they share one sentence in the book:
Single muscle cells — deformations exceeding 80% consistently ruptured cell membranes, causing immediate and irreversible damage.
Whole muscle — 2 hours of sustained deformation at strains higher than 50% inflicted irreversible damage.
Different preparations, different thresholds, different time courses. Build them adjacent and labelled by preparation or they will be remembered as one number.

coverage-20260920-deep-injury.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 46
coverage-20260920-deep-injury.auditText: THE SENTENCE THAT IS DEEP TISSUE PRESSURE INJURY IN ONE LINE: muscle tissue is metabolically active, and when ischaemic it is more sensitive to deformation forces, so IRREVERSIBLE DAMAGE MAY BE PRESENT AT THE MUSCLE LAYER WITHOUT SUCH DAMAGE OCCURRING IN THE SKIN OR SUBCUTANEOUS LAYERS. Cell death and local necrosis then change tissue geometry, which further increases deformation force and exacerbates the injury. Heat accumulation or increased skin temperature intensifies ischaemia and hypoxia because it raises metabolic rate and oxygen demand. Inflammation raises interstitial fluid pressure, impeding arteriolar circulation; capillaries collapse and thrombosis occurs; lymphatic flow decreases, allowing oedema and contributing to necrosis.

coverage-20260920-pressure-shear-frictio.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 46
coverage-20260920-pressure-shear-frictio.auditText: SHEAR VERSUS FRICTION, and the distinction is examinable: shear stress is a PARALLEL force, in contrast to pressure which is PERPENDICULAR; shear stress leads to tissue deformation or distortion called shear strain; shear deforms the cell membrane, stretches tissues and displaces blood vessels laterally. FRICTION is a superficial force applied to the skin and IS NOT CONSIDERED A TRUE CAUSE OF PI, though it damages the upper layers and makes skin less tolerant of the other forces; chronic friction injuries occur in patients who slide out of chairs to stand or move between surfaces, and the tissue becomes hyperkeratotic and often hyperpigmented — AND THESE TISSUE CHANGES ARE NOT CLASSIFIED AS PI.

coverage-20260920-tissue-tolerance.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 46
coverage-20260920-tissue-tolerance.auditText: TOLERANCE FOR PRESSURE: protein-calorie malnutrition with low BMI reduces the adipose padding over bony prominences; undernourished patients also have longer ICU stays, reduced functional status, higher acuity, more comorbidity and higher mortality; OBESITY ALSO CREATES RISK. SCAR TISSUE HAS TENSILE STRENGTH OF 40% THAT OF NATIVE TISSUE, so a patient with a prior stage 4 sacral PI has scar tissue at increased risk of future injury there.

coverage-20260920-four-mechanisms.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 46
coverage-20260920-four-mechanisms.auditText: THE FOUR HYPOTHESES FOR PI PATHOPHYSIOLOGY, as printed and numbered: 1, high-magnitude pressure leading to direct deformation of tissue cells. 2, ischaemia caused by capillary occlusion. 3, shear leading to ischaemia of tissues. 4, reduced tolerance for pressure from comorbid conditions such as malnutrition, arterial disease, neuropathic conditions, exposure to moisture, or previous full-thickness injury to the skin.

coverage-20260920-support-surfaces.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 46
coverage-20260920-support-surfaces.auditText:
SUPPORT SURFACES, from the NPIAP support surface initiative. Premise: if pressure is redistributed over a larger body area the relative pressure at any one area is less — the book's own analogy is pushing your hand onto a surface of many nails versus one nail, which is worth keeping because it makes the concept stick.
REACTIVE surfaces are powered or nonpowered surfaces able to change load distribution properties ONLY IN RESPONSE TO AN APPLIED LOAD; they reduce pressure by immersion and envelopment of the body into the surface. A FOAM MATTRESS is a nonpowered reactive surface.
ACTIVE surfaces are POWERED surfaces that inflate and deflate cells of air to change pressure over a body area, reducing pressure by periodically shifting the areas of support so deformation is not sustained over one area. AN ALTERNATING AIR MATTRESS is an active powered surface. Active surfaces are generally recommended for persons at higher risk when FREQUENT REPOSITIONING IS NOT POSSIBLE.
INTRAOPERATIVE PI: clinicians should advocate for support surfaces in the operating room. High-risk patients are those whose OPERATION WILL EXCEED 3 HOURS, those with ASA SCORES OF 3 OR HIGHER, and those PRONE FOR SURGERY. Exposed areas vary by position; staff familiar with the position should place prophylactic dressings on high-risk areas or pad the table.

coverage-20260920-canes.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 55
coverage-20260920-canes.auditText: CANES, p1800 region. Most popular mobility aid for older adults, lightweight and easy where space is limited. PROPER HEIGHT IS THE HANDLE AT THE LEVEL OF THE WRIST WHEN THE ARM IS FULLY EXTENDED. THE CANE IS USED IN THE HAND ON THE SIDE OPPOSITE THE INVOLVED EXTREMITY — and the chapter says outright that many people incorrectly use it on the same side, where it acts as a brace instead of unloading the limb. Gait: hold the cane opposite the involved extremity and ADVANCE THE CANE AND THE INVOLVED EXTREMITY TOGETHER, bearing weight on the cane and to a lesser degree on the involved extremity. STAIRS: THE UNINVOLVED EXTREMITY GOES UP FIRST while the involved extremity and cane remain on the lower step; TO DESCEND, THE INVOLVED EXTREMITY AND THE CANE ARE LOWERED FIRST. In persons with decreased lower extremity sensation a cane also provides sensory feedback. Straight versus quad: quad canes are aluminium with a four-legged base; the advantage is the cane does not fall if the person releases the handle; the disadvantage of some quad canes is that the base is too large to place on a stair.

coverage-20260920-crutches.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 55
coverage-20260920-crutches.auditText: CRUTCHES. USUALLY NOT USED WITH OLDER ADULTS because a higher level of coordination and skill is required. Two types, axillary and forearm. IF AXILLARY CRUTCHES ARE USED INCORRECTLY, SHOULDER INJURY AND/OR AXILLARY NERVE DAMAGE CAN OCCUR. Forearm crutches are more functional because a cuff secures the crutch on the arm, freeing the hand to manipulate objects. Crutches usually give bilateral support, but a single crutch can replace a cane where additional unilateral support is needed.

coverage-20260920-walkers.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 55
coverage-20260920-walkers.auditText:
WALKERS. Prescribed when a cane does not provide sufficient support; bilateral support, easier than crutches; adjust so the user maintains an ERECT POSTURE and is not required to lean forward to reach the walker.
Standard four-point or "pick-up" walker — must be picked up with each step, requiring arm strength and endurance, producing a slow walking speed.
Two-wheeled rolling walker — a more normal gait pattern and speed; HAVING TWO RATHER THAN THREE OR FOUR WHEELS PROVIDES MORE STABILITY.
Four-wheeled walker, the "rollator" — hand brakes so it can be locked when standing up and sitting down, a platform seat for resting, a basket; REQUIRES GREATER SKILL because of the hand brakes; PREFERRED FOR OUTDOOR USE because the larger wheels move more easily over sidewalks and slightly rough terrain.
Merry Walker — maximal support, front, side and back bars and a seat; larger and harder to manoeuvre in homes; often used in institutional settings for persons with severe balance and coordination deficits.
The stability ordering here is counterintuitive and is the reason this belongs as a comparison block rather than a list: MORE wheels is not MORE stable.

coverage-20260920-wheelchairs.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 55
coverage-20260920-wheelchairs.auditText:
WHEELCHAIRS. Prescribed when a person can no longer walk safely or walking endurance is low; allows activities such as shopping that need extended standing and walking, maintaining quality of life and avoiding social isolation. Stability and mobility both matter: A BACK HEIGHT TOO HIGH MAKES PROPELLING THE CHAIR INDEPENDENTLY DIFFICULT AND IMPAIRS MOBILITY, TOO LOW MAY NOT PROVIDE ADEQUATE TRUNK SUPPORT. Removable armrests and footrests make transfers easier and safer; FIXED FOOTRESTS ARE NOT RECOMMENDED BECAUSE THEY CAN CONTRIBUTE TO FALLS. Consultation with the occupational or physical therapist is recommended. Manual chairs are lighter and fold into a car; power chairs and scooters give enhanced outdoor and community mobility but most are difficult to manoeuvre in homes and need a car carrier.
THE TRADE-OFF TO STATE PLAINLY: for patients who are able to walk, having a wheelchair may discourage walking, leading to decreased muscle strength and endurance.

coverage-20260920-pd-freezing-depression.source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, chapter 61
coverage-20260920-pd-freezing-depression.auditText:
ONE THING FROM p2052 YOU DO NOT HAVE, printed immediately after the antimuscarinic sentence: exposure to antimuscarinic drugs has been linked to a higher risk of developing FREEZING OF GAIT in PD. That belongs with the avoidance statement, not separately — it converts a side-effect caution into a second, motor reason to avoid the class.
Also from p2052-2053, on PD depression: bupropion and tricyclic antidepressants are useful; if insomnia is also a problem, an antidepressant that is also a soporific is doubly advantageous — nortriptyline, WHICH HAS FEWER ANTICHOLINERGIC EFFECTS THAN AMITRIPTYLINE, or low-dose mirtazapine; and recent data suggest CBT may improve PD depression more than existing medication-based approaches.

uro-20260920-mechanics.auditText: NORMAL MICTURITION MECHANICS, p1548: as the bladder fills, bladder pressure remains low, at or below 15 cm H2O. THE BLADDER VOLUME AT FIRST URGE TO VOID IS VARIABLE BUT GENERALLY OCCURS AT BETWEEN 150 AND 350 mL; normal bladder capacity is 300 to 600 mL. This RESOLVES a pending item — the sentence you have was truncated at "between 150" and the reader already carries the capacity figure without its partner. Pending list drops to four. When normal urination is initiated, usually every 3 to 4 hours during wakefulness, THE DETRUSOR CONTRACTS AND DETRUSOR PRESSURE INCREASES UNTIL IT EXCEEDS URETHRAL RESISTANCE, which lowers immediately prior to bladder contraction. Urine flow occurs typically over less than 2 minutes. IF AT ANY TIME DURING FILLING TOTAL BLADDER PRESSURE EXCEEDS OUTLET RESISTANCE, LEAKAGE OCCURS — transmitted intra-abdominal pressure from coughing or sneezing may cause leakage in someone with low outlet resistance or urethral sphincter weakness; alternatively the bladder can contract involuntarily.

uro-20260920-age-related.auditText: AGE-RELATED CHANGES, p1549-1550: postvoid residual volume is greater with increasing age. Reduced functional bladder capacity is associated with advanced age but may be due to the higher prevalence of involuntary bladder contractions and detrusor overactivity. DETRUSOR OVERACTIVITY HAS BEEN ASSOCIATED WITH SPECIFIC ANATOMICAL FINDINGS ON BLADDER BIOPSY — protrusion junctions and ultra-close abutment of detrusor muscle cells — AND WITH CORTICAL CHANGES SUGGESTING IMPAIRED INTEGRATION OF BLADDER AFFERENT SIGNALS. Involuntary contractions do not always cause incontinence, but combined with impaired mobility they likely account for a substantial proportion of incontinence in functionally disabled older patients. Aging in women is associated with a decline in bladder outlet and urethral resistance pressure. Prior childbirths, vaginal or Caesarean, are associated with greater risk of future incontinence, BUT THIS ASSOCIATION IS WEAKER FOR WOMEN OLDER THAN 65. In older populations POOR VAGINAL SUPPORT IS MORE CLOSELY ASSOCIATED WITH OBSTRUCTIVE URINARY SYMPTOMS THAN WITH LEAKAGE AND URGENCY. Obesity, deconditioned muscles and hysterectomy predispose to future incontinence. White women as a group are more likely to have stress urinary incontinence than women of other racial or ethnic groups. ORAL ESTROGEN THERAPY HAS BEEN IDENTIFIED AS A RISK FACTOR FOR SUBSEQUENT DEVELOPMENT OF URINARY INCONTINENCE — counterintuitive and therefore examinable. Older men with prostatic enlargement may have decreased urine flow rates and detrusor muscle instability. Aging is associated with more frequent nocturia, partly from higher night-time urine production.

uro-20260920-dhic.auditText: THE ENTITY THAT IS ENTIRELY ABSENT AND IS A STANDARD GERIATRICS EXAM ITEM: DETRUSOR HYPERACTIVITY WITH IMPAIRED CONTRACTILITY. Many older men and women have detrusor hyperactivity combined with poor bladder contractility, termed exactly that. These individuals have evidence of WIDESPREAD MUSCLE DEGENERATION ON DETRUSOR MUSCLE BIOPSY. A subgroup of older incontinent patients with detrusor hyperactivity also have impaired bladder contractility, EMPTYING LESS THAN ONE-THIRD OF THEIR BLADDER VOLUME WITH INVOLUNTARY CONTRACTIONS ON URODYNAMIC TESTING; they may be PREDISPOSED TO SIGNIFICANT URINARY RETENTION and may require training to learn to empty completely. Build this as its own named entity, not as a sentence inside the urgency section. The clinical picture is wet and retaining at the same time, which is the thing that catches people out.

uro-20260920-urgency-dyssynergia.auditText: Also: urgency incontinence is most often BUT NOT ALWAYS associated with involuntary bladder contractions — some patients have a POORLY COMPLIANT BLADDER WITHOUT INVOLUNTARY CONTRACTIONS, for example interstitial cystitis or following irradiation. And lesions rostral to the lumbosacral spinal cord, such as multiple sclerosis, cause DETRUSOR-SPHINCTER DYSSYNERGIA with consequent urinary retention, treated similarly to overflow incontinence, with sphincterotomy occasionally necessary.

uro-20260920-eye-examination.auditText: EYE MOVEMENTS, p2127 region: vertical gaze abnormality progressing to complete palsy WITH A PRESERVED OCULOCEPHALIC REFLEX is characteristic of PSP. HORIZONTAL GAZE ABNORMALITIES ARE MORE TYPICAL OF CBD. That pair is a discriminator and belongs as a contrast. Saccadic abnormalities occur across disorders from AD to PSP. Technique as printed: ask the patient to focus on an object in front of them, such as a pen tip held by the examiner, then quickly refocus on an item in the peripheral field such as the examiner's finger, watching for SACCADIC LATENCY (delay in initiation), INCOMPLETE SACCADES (gaze palsy), and INTERRUPTED OR JERKY SACCADIC MOVEMENT. SACCADES SHOULD BE TESTED IN ALL FOUR DIRECTIONS. Test ocular pursuit separately by having the patient track an object horizontally and vertically. Also from the chapter: examination should probe cognition, behaviour and movement with emphasis on the EARLIEST abnormalities, because early symptoms reflect where the illness began and that is usually helpful in determining disease etiology.

uro-20260920-stroke-caa.auditText:
SEIZURES AND EPILEPSY IN OLDER ADULTS, and this whole section is absent: acute and remote strokes are common causes. WHEN A NEW SEIZURE DEVELOPS IN THE SETTING OF A STROKE THE CAUSE IS GENERALLY HEMORRHAGIC, whereas both hemorrhagic and ischaemic strokes can cause chronic seizures. A common cause of hemorrhagic stroke is hypertension, HOWEVER HYPERTENSION GENERALLY CAUSES HEMORRHAGES IN DEEP BRAIN STRUCTURES, THUS HYPERTENSION IS NOT THE MOST COMMON CAUSE OF STROKES ASSOCIATED WITH SEIZURES. CORTICAL hemorrhages commonly occur in CEREBRAL AMYLOID ANGIOPATHY, characterised by amyloid deposition in the small vessels of both brain and leptomeninges — the same abnormal protein that accumulates in AD, with or without parenchymal deposition — and CAA predisposes to small microbleeds and larger intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhages. That chain, cortical location to CAA rather than hypertension, is the teaching point and must be built as a chain rather than as separate facts.
Brain tumours are another common cause. Although primary brain tumours can cause seizures, METASTATIC LESIONS ARE THE MOST COMMON TYPE OF INTRACRANIAL TUMOUR PRESENTING WITH EPILEPSY IN OLDER PERSONS; tumours that most often metastasise to brain originate from LUNG, BREAST, KIDNEY, COLON, RECTUM AND SKIN (MELANOMA).
Encephalitis due to underlying autoimmune or paraneoplastic disease commonly presents with SUBACUTE COGNITIVE OR BEHAVIOURAL CHANGES AND SEIZURES and requires direct antibody testing for diagnosis; treatment requires immunosuppressive drugs in addition to antiepileptics, plus identification and treatment of underlying malignancy. Given the higher prevalence of valvular heart disease and cardiac surgery, infections can present with septic emboli or CNS abscesses from endocarditis and present with epilepsy.

primary-uro-lecanemab.auditText: FDA converted lecanemab to traditional approval on July 6, 2023 after a confirmatory trial verified clinical benefit. Initiation is for mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to AD, with confirmed amyloid pathology. The trial showed slower decline. The warning covers ARIA, sometimes serious or life-threatening, and intracerebral bleeding. This does not establish prevention in asymptomatic people or efficacy against delirium.

primary-uro-donanemab.auditText: The letter grants approval for donanemab for AD; its electronic signature on PDF page 11 is dated July 2, 2024. FDA’s companion approval announcement states initiation in mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia, confirmed amyloid pathology in the studied population, slower clinical decline, and a boxed ARIA warning.

primary-uro-aduhelm.auditText: Biogen announced discontinuation of aducanumab development and commercialization and termination of ENVISION. The company stated this decision was not related to safety or efficacy concerns. This is a manufacturer discontinuation announcement, not an FDA withdrawal finding.

primary-uro-autoimmune.auditText: A clinical approach to diagnosis of autoimmune encephalitis. DOI 10.1016/S1474-4422(15)00401-9. Antibody absence does not exclude immune-mediated encephalitis; a positive result alone does not establish it. The criteria include antibody-negative probable AE and some definite limbic encephalitis without antibodies. Antibody testing remains important to identify subtypes and associated tumours. Reviewed manuscript pages 3, 6 and 16 (PDF indexes 2, 5 and 15).

primary-uro-stroke.auditText: European Stroke Organisation guidelines for management of post-stroke seizures and epilepsy. DOI 10.1177/2396987317705536. Acute symptomatic seizure incidence is higher after intracranial haemorrhage than ischaemic stroke; both cause seizures. Cortical involvement is an independent risk factor. A conditional risk within a stroke type does not establish that most stroke-associated seizure cases have that type. Reviewed abstract and introduction.

infection-sleep-colonisation.auditText: PIs are colonised with bacteria, and the longer a wound is open and unhealed the greater the risk of biofilm. PIs are typically colonised with GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO 10^5 ORGANISMS/mL of normal skin flora. Although that level can cause local infection in intact skin and impair healing in surgical wounds, CHRONIC WOUNDS SUCH AS PI MAY BEAR MICROBIAL GROWTH AT THIS LEVEL FOR PROLONGED PERIODS WITHOUT NOTICEABLE CLINICAL INFECTION AND WITH EVIDENCE OF SOME HEALING — the same number means something different in a chronic wound than in intact skin or a surgical wound, and that is the teaching point, not the number.
infection-sleep-colonisation.method: Supplied review; no independent PDF read by builder. Page or regional range anchored by the existing page-cited index and earlier user page audit; a range is not a pinpoint locator for every sentence.

infection-sleep-mmp.auditText: While not healing, the wound stays inflamed. Chronic inflammation impairs healing because proinflammatory cytokines — INTERLEUKIN 1 AND TUMOUR NECROSIS FACTOR — increase matrix metalloproteinases. MMPs are a family of CALCIUM-DEPENDENT ZINC-CONTAINING ENZYMES that degrade extracellular matrix; they play a crucial role in ALL stages of wound healing by modifying the wound matrix to allow cell migration and tissue remodelling; but in chronic wounds there is EXCESSIVE expression of MMPs, which retards healing while promoting ongoing inflammation. The same enzyme family is necessary and harmful depending on quantity — build it that way.
infection-sleep-mmp.method: Supplied review; no independent PDF read by builder. Page or regional range anchored by the existing page-cited index and earlier user page audit; a range is not a pinpoint locator for every sentence.

infection-sleep-biofilm.auditText: Biofilms are microbial communities in which bacteria are encased in EXOPOLYSACCHARIDE (EPS) and are LESS METABOLICALLY ACTIVE than their free-living counterparts. CLINICAL STUDIES SHOW 60% OF CHRONIC WOUNDS CONTAIN A BIOFILM. Biofilms promote chronic inflammation. The nature of the EPS makes biofilms very resistant to endogenous antibodies and phagocytic cells AND to exogenous antibiotics and antimicrobial solutions. Bacterial biofilms may be the underlying pathology preventing PIs from healing. BIOFILM IS NOT VISIBLE TO THE NAKED EYE BUT SHOULD BE SUSPECTED IN ALL CHRONIC WOUNDS. The best method of prevention is adequate, timely and complete debridement of necrotic tissue followed by appropriate topical therapy. CADEXOMER IODINE, MEDICAL-GRADE HONEY, SILVER AND POLYHEXAMETHYLENE BIGUANIDE (PHMB) dressings retard development of new biofilm. REGARDLESS OF TOPICAL TREATMENT THE BIOFILM WILL REFORM, AND MAINTENANCE DEBRIDEMENT IS REQUIRED.
infection-sleep-biofilm.method: Supplied review; no independent PDF read by builder. Page or regional range anchored by the existing page-cited index and earlier user page audit; a range is not a pinpoint locator for every sentence.

infection-sleep-infection.auditText:
Infection is a common cause of nonhealing or worsening PI. PIs are chronic ischaemic wounds, so they are more susceptible to infection, and they occur in malnourished or poorly perfused patients who cannot mount a full immune response. MOST COMMON ORGANISMS: STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS, PROTEUS MIRABILIS, PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA, ENTEROCOCCUS FAECALIS. Infected PI can serve as reservoirs for antibiotic-resistant bacteria; MRSA colonisation in infected PI is now reported commonly.
DIAGNOSIS: stage 3, 4 and unstageable PI should be evaluated for acute and chronic infection. TISSUE BIOPSY OR QUANTITATIVE SWAB to determine wound tissue bioburden is the preferred method. DO NOT RELY ON CULTURES OF THE WOUND SURFACE OR WOUND DRAINAGE — they present only surface contamination. Tissue biopsy is the gold standard but is not always feasible. LEVINE'S TECHNIQUE uses light pressure on the wound bed to draw wound fluid for culture.
infection-sleep-infection.method: Supplied review; no independent PDF read by builder. Page or regional range anchored by the existing page-cited index and earlier user page audit; a range is not a pinpoint locator for every sentence.

infection-sleep-osteomyelitis.auditText: REPORTED IN 32% OF PATIENTS WITH STAGE 4 PI. THE STRONGEST CLINICAL INDICATOR IS PALPABLE SOFT OR ROUGH BONE, OR VISIBLE BONE. Most infections are POLYMICROBIAL with a predominance of S aureus, Enterobacteriaceae spp. and anaerobes. Plain film x-ray is useful for identifying probable osteomyelitis, but FINAL DIAGNOSIS IS BEST MADE FROM MRI AND BONE BIOPSY WITH CULTURES. Management includes surgical debridement of infected bone plus antibiotics; duration varies by level of infection, and infection limited to cortical bone may not require a full 6 weeks. Antibiotics are not risk free and often cause diarrhoea, further contaminating the wound bed. WHERE EXPOSURE TO FAECAL MATTER CANNOT BE CONTROLLED AND THE PI IS CONTAMINATED BY IT, FAECAL DIVERSION WITH CATHETERS AND DIVERTING COLOSTOMY SHOULD BE CONSIDERED.
infection-sleep-osteomyelitis.method: Supplied review; no independent PDF read by builder. Page or regional range anchored by the existing page-cited index and earlier user page audit; a range is not a pinpoint locator for every sentence.

infection-sleep-surgery.auditText: In patients with large infected PI, or who cannot improve limb perfusion, amputation and hemicorporectomy are sometimes required. SURGICAL COMPLICATION RATES — dehiscence, infection, necrosis, haematoma — for both younger paraplegic and nonparaplegic older patients are AS HIGH AS 50%. PI RECURRENCE AT THE SAME SITE RANGES FROM 30% TO 70%. Even so, 70% TO 80% OF SURGICALLY TREATED PI ARE HEALED ON DISCHARGE. Recurrence at the same site is LOWER for older patients (40%) than for younger paraplegic patients (MORE THAN 70%), but 30% OF OLDER PATIENTS DEVELOP NEW INJURY SITES, and MORTALITY IN OLDER PATIENTS RANGES FROM NEARLY 50% TO 68%. Keep the same-site recurrence figures paired and labelled by population — 40% versus more than 70% is a contrast, and separated by a screen they become one remembered number.

infection-sleep-healing.auditText: PARTIAL-THICKNESS (STAGE 2) SHOULD HEAL WITHIN 60 DAYS MAXIMUM; FULL-THICKNESS (STAGE 3, 4, UNSTAGEABLE) SHOULD DEMONSTRATE IMPROVEMENT IN OVERALL INJURY STATUS EVERY 2 TO 4 WEEKS. Documentation must include risk status, prevention strategies, assessment (size, stage, location and description of the wound bed as a minimum), treatment plan, and evaluation of treatment success.

infection-sleep-pain.auditText: Of persons with PI able to report pain: 87% REPORT PAIN WITH DRESSING CHANGES, 84% PAIN AT REST, 42% PAIN BOTH AT REST AND DURING DRESSING CHANGES. 18% of those reporting dressing-change pain report it at the highest level, described as excruciating. AND ONLY 6% OF PERSONS REPORTING PI PAIN RECEIVE ANY MEDICATION FOR PAIN. Higher proportions of stage 3 or 4 injuries report pain, and more severe pain, than stage 2. The Joint Commission estimates 2.5 million patients in acute care hospitals are treated for PI each year.

infection-sleep-hypoglossal.auditText: an implanted lead goes to the respiratory muscles to sense onset of inspiration, and a second lead to the hypoglossal nerve causes TONGUE CONTRACTION TO OPEN THE AIRWAY with inspiration, through direct action and through MUSCULAR COUPLING WITH THE SOFT PALATE. Randomised trials found promising results IN A HIGHLY SELECTED GROUP WITH BMI LESS THAN 32 kg/m2 WHO COULD NOT TOLERATE CPAP. Initial trials had limited numbers of older patients. A RECENT COHORT STUDY OF 62 PATIENTS AGED 65 TO 80 FOUND SIGNIFICANT REDUCTIONS IN AHI AND SLEEPINESS SCORES in this population.

A more aggressive approach is maxillary mandibular advancement.

A POLYSOMNOGRAM IS REQUIRED to define PLMS and thus diagnose PLMD. Build the three percentages and the exclusion rule as one block; the percentages exist to justify the exclusion.

THE RBD MAY BE WORSENED BY THE USE OF SSRIs TO TREAT CATAPLEXY. Other neurologic disorders associated with RBD include cerebrovascular disease, multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, normal pressure hydrocephalus and Tourette syndrome.

primary-infection-sleep-whs.auditText: Validated quantitative wound swabs are an alternative to tissue biopsy after debridement. Osteomyelitis requires bone culture and histology; imaging is less definitive. Confirmed disease is treated with debridement and culture-guided antibiotics. Diversion may help selected sacral/ischial wounds but surgery is not always needed and carries substantial risk. Radical surgery is rare. Stable dry heel eschar without inflammation or infection need not be debrided. Systemic antibiotics are for sepsis, spreading cellulitis or osteomyelitis, not colonisation alone.
